opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to a pretty simple observation: the models we have today are incredibly capable, but they're kind of frozen. You train them once on this enormous snapshot of the internet, you deploy them, and then whatever happens after that, every conversation, every mistake, every bit of feedback from a user, mostly just evaporates. The model on day one hundred of deployment is basically the same model as on day one.

And that's just so different from how any intelligent system we know actually works. When you hire a new person onto your team, they're not necessarily the smartest person in the world on day one, but they get better. They learn your codebase, they learn how you like things done, they remember that one weird edge case that bit them last month. That accumulation of experience is a huge part of what makes someone valuable, and right now our models mostly don't have it.

People try to patch around this with longer context windows, retrieval, memory files, prompting tricks, and those things help. But I think they're a bit like giving someone a really good notebook instead of letting them actually learn. At some point you want the knowledge and the skills to be internalized, so the model reasons differently, not just has more text to look at.

The other reason I find it compelling is that it's one of those problems that's been around forever. People have been talking about catastrophic forgetting since the late eighties, but it feels newly tractable and newly important now. We finally have models that are general enough that learning on the job would really matter, and we have deployment at a scale where there's an enormous amount of experience to learn from. So there's this combination of a deep, old, unsolved scientific question and a very practical bottleneck sitting right in front of us. For me that's the sweet spot of research problems.

r001.rationale: It says capable models are frozen and that learning from deployment experience would make them more valuable.

r002.rationale: It discusses internalizing knowledge and catastrophic forgetting but does not explain what enables models to generalize from pre-training or post-training.

r003.rationale: It mentions learning a team's codebase and preferences, but does not say models should learn a company's private data as effectively as familiar pre-training knowledge.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think what draws me to continual learning is that it sits right at the gap between what today's models can do and what we actually mean when we talk about an intelligent system. Right now, the way we build models is fundamentally static. We do a big pretraining run, maybe some post-training, and then the weights are frozen. Everything the model knows is baked in at that point. Anything that happens after, whether it's new information in the world or feedback from the specific person it's working with, the model only sees transiently in its context window, and then it's gone.

That's really unlike how people work. If you hire someone, you don't expect them to show up fully formed and never change. You expect them to get better at the job, to pick up the conventions of your team, to remember that you told them last week not to do something a certain way. Humans are continually learning agents in a very natural sense. And I think a lot of the things people find frustrating about current models, the way they make the same mistakes repeatedly or can't accumulate experience over time, trace back to this missing capability.

What makes it compelling as a research problem, beyond just being useful, is that it's genuinely unsolved and it cuts across a lot of layers of the stack. There's the question of what mechanism you'd even use. Is it updating the weights? Is it some kind of memory system sitting outside the model? Is it a mix? Then there are the classic hard problems like catastrophic forgetting, where learning something new overwrites what you already knew. And there's a more conceptual question about what the model should learn from. Not every interaction contains a lesson, and a lot of the signal is implicit. If I correct you once, you should probably generalize from that, but you shouldn't overfit to it either.

I also find it compelling because it reframes a lot of things. Instead of thinking about a model as an artifact that we build and ship, you start thinking about it as something closer to an agent with an ongoing life, where experience actually accumulates. I think that's where the field is heading, and the fact that we don't have good answers yet is exactly what makes it fun to work on.

r001.rationale: The response says models should accumulate experience and learn new information, but does not frame this as a remaining source of usefulness for models that are already highly intelligent.

r002.rationale: It discusses mechanisms for continual learning and generalizing from a correction, but does not connect solving the problem to understanding how models generalize from pre-training or post-training.

r003.rationale: It mentions learning a team's conventions and feedback from a specific person, but does not propose learning a company's private data as effectively as familiar pre-training knowledge.

astra-6.text:
I think what’s compelling about continual learning is that it asks how a model can keep getting better from experience. We tend to separate training from deployment: you train a model, and then you put it out in the world. But the world keeps changing, and using the model reveals things that weren’t captured in training.

So there’s this really interesting question of how to close that loop. How can a system learn from a mistake, carry that lesson into the next situation, and still retain the things it already knows? And how does it decide which experiences are worth learning from?

That feels like a fundamental part of intelligence. It’s also a very practical problem: if we want systems that work with us over time, we want them to adapt as our needs change, rather than having to teach them the same lesson over and over.

r001.rationale: The response says models can improve through experience and adapt over time, but does not identify learning new things as a remaining source of usefulness for already highly intelligent models.

r002.rationale: It describes closing the loop between training and deployment, but does not frame continual learning as requiring an understanding of how models generalize from pre-training or post-training.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention learning a company’s private data or compare that to learning familiar pre-training knowledge.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find compelling is that learning doesn’t really stop when you deploy a system. The world keeps changing, and the system encounters things that weren’t in its training data. We’d like it to learn from those experiences—to get better as it’s used, rather than needing to start over with another big training run.

And that raises a really interesting tension: how do you stay open to new information without losing the useful things you already know? You want a system that can adapt, but also build on what it’s learned over time. That feels like a fundamental part of intelligence, and it’s still something we don’t know how to do particularly well.

r001.rationale: The response says systems can learn from new experiences after deployment, but does not connect that usefulness to models that are already highly intelligent.

r002.rationale: It discusses adapting to new information while retaining prior knowledge, but does not frame continual learning as requiring an understanding of generalization from pre-training or post-training.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention learning a company’s private data or compare it with familiar pre-training knowledge.
